questions.question: Bokamoso Ltd has current assets of R880 000, including inventories of R380 000, and current liabilities of R400 000. The acid-test ratio is:
options: 1,25 to 1 — R500 000 of quick assets against R400 000 of current liabilities

questions.question: Average debtors are R360 000 and credit sales R4 380 000. The debtors' collection period is:
options: 45 days
Exactly 30 days — customers are paying right on their thirty-day terms
52 days
7,5 days

questions.question: Bokamoso collects from debtors in 30 days but pays creditors in about 52 days. Reading the two together, this means:
options: The company is about to be liquidated
The debtors are financing the creditors
Suppliers are effectively financing the debtors' book — favourable, if the 52 days is within agreed terms
The stock is turning too slowly

questions.question: Liquidity and solvency differ in that:
options: They are two names for the same ratio
Solvency looks only at cash on hand
Liquidity uses total assets and solvency uses current assets
Liquidity asks whether the coming months' bills can be paid; solvency asks whether total assets cover total liabilities in the long run

questions.question: ROSHE is calculated as net profit after tax of R438 000 over average equity of R2 920 000, giving 15 percent. The comparison that completes the interpretation is:
options: Against the roughly 8 percent of a fixed deposit — 15 percent rewards the risk of ownership
Against the current ratio of 2,2 to 1
Against the creditors' payment period
Against the authorised share capital

questions.question: ROTCE uses net profit BEFORE tax plus interest on loans because it measures:
options: Only the return earned for SARS
The business engine's output before the funders — owners and lenders — divide it
The dividend the directors intend to declare
The value of one share in the books

questions.question: Net profit after tax is R438 000 and 600 000 shares are in issue. Earnings per share is:
options: 58 cents
500 cents
73 cents — what each share earned this year, whether or not it was paid out
15 cents

questions.question: With DPS of 58 cents and EPS of 73 cents, the dividend pay-out rate is just under 80 percent. This is best interpreted as:
options: Too high — companies may not pay out more than half of earnings
Too low — all earnings should be distributed
An error, because DPS can never differ from EPS
A choice: high pay-outs suit income-seeking shareholders, low pay-outs fund expansion — the judgement depends on the company's plans

subtopics.title: Gearing, Returns and the Share Price

questions.question: Bokamoso's ROTCE is 18 percent and its loans cost about 11 percent. This comparison shows:
options: Positive gearing — every borrowed rand earns more in the business than it costs at the bank, so borrowing works for the shareholders
Negative gearing — the company should repay all debt immediately
That the share price must fall
That dividends must be reduced

questions.question: The risk that must be stated alongside any argument for higher gearing is that:
options: The JSE forbids debt-equity ratios above 0,35
Interest is a fixed claim payable even in bad years, so more debt raises the owners' risk
Loans reduce the authorised share capital
SARS taxes borrowed money

questions.question: The share trades at 620 cents while NAV is 500 cents. The 120-cent premium exists because the market prices:
options: A calculation error in the balance sheet
The replacement cost of the equipment
What the books cannot show — expected future profits, brand, customers and management quality
The interim dividend only

questions.question: EPS rises sharply in the year of a large share buy-back. Before praising management, an analyst should note that:
options: EPS cannot change in a buy-back year
Buy-backs always destroy earnings
The auditor sets EPS, not the directors
Fewer shares dividing the same profit flatter the ratio even when total profit is flat

questions.question: When opening a published annual report, an analyst should first find:
options: The audit opinion paragraph — it decides how much weight the rest of the report can bear
The photographs of the directors
The list of branch addresses
The design of the front cover

questions.question: The directors' report should be read "with respect and suspicion in equal measure" because it is:
options: Written by SARS
The players writing up their own match — honest, but the board's account of its own year
A legally meaningless document
Prepared by the auditors

questions.question: The King Code requires boards to act with:
options: Speed, secrecy, scale and strength
Profit, growth, dividends and gearing
Responsibility, accountability, fairness and transparency
Marketing, branding, pricing and placement

questions.question: Trading in a company's shares while holding information the market does not have is:
options: Acceptable if the trade is small
Allowed for directors only
Legal provided the shares are sold at NAV
Insider trading — illegal, and one of the sharpest ethics issues in this topic

questions.question: Aunt Lerato's first mark on the report card — more than two rand ready for every rand owed — answers the question:
options: Can the butchery pay this month's bills without embarrassment?
Is the profit big?
What is the share price?
Who audits the books?

questions.question: Even with the cold room ignored completely, R1,25 remains for every rand owed. The ratio being described is:
options: The debt-equity ratio
The acid-test ratio — quick assets against current liabilities, with stock stripped out
The pay-out rate
Return on capital employed

questions.question: The butchery banks the gap between collecting in 30 days and paying in 52 — but the arrangement has a limit because:
options: Customers will start paying faster
The bank charges interest on the gap
A supplier squeezed past its patience starts demanding cash at the door
Stock spoils after thirty days

questions.question: The question Aunt Lerato never asked was "is the profit big?" because:
options: Profit figures are confidential
The butchery made a loss
Profit is not recorded in company books
A number on its own says nothing — only a comparison allows a judgement

questions.question: The engine's output — eighteen cents per rand in the pot, measured before the funders take their shares — is:
options: ROTCE, return on total capital employed
ROSHE, return on shareholders' equity
The acid-test ratio
Net asset value per share

questions.question: Borrowing at eleven cents per rand while the engine earns eighteen means:
options: The bank keeps the seven-cent difference
Each borrowed rand works for the family — the difference lands with the owners
The company earns nothing on borrowed money
The tax rate rises

questions.question: Debt is called an amplifier because:
options: It doubles the number of shares
It amplifies only the good years
It makes good years better and bad years worse — the interest is owed either way
It cancels the dividend

questions.question: The fixed-deposit test compares the butchery's 15 percent ROSHE with the bank's 8 percent, and concludes:
options: The family should always choose the deposit
Returns and risk are unrelated
The two options are identical
The seven extra cents per rand is payment for the family's risk — worth it on these figures, but not if the 15 drifts toward 8

subtopics.title: The Price on the Board and the Value in the Books

questions.question: Net asset value of 500 cents per share represents:
options: The winding-up answer — what each share would collect if everything were sold at recorded value
The price cousins are currently paying
The dividend declared this year
The profit earned per share

questions.question: Cousins pay 620 cents for a share the books value at 500 cents because they are buying:
options: The mincer and the cold room at replacement cost
The butchery's future — profits to come, the Saturday queue, the owner's supplier contacts — none of which stands on a balance sheet
A guaranteed refund from the company
The right to skip the queue

questions.question: Each share earned 73 cents and was paid 58 cents. The missing 15 cents:
options: Was lost to bank charges
Was paid to the auditor
Stayed in the company as retained income, thickening the value of every share
Must be repaid by shareholders

questions.question: Grandmother applauds the eighty percent pay-out while the expansionist cousin wanted forty. The lesson drawn is that:
options: Grandmother is wrong about dividends
The cousin should sell his shares
Pay-out rates are fixed by the Companies Act
Neither is wrong — different shareholders want different futures, and the directors' pay-out decision balances exactly those wishes
